If an object floats, its specific gravity is less than one. If it sinks, its specific gravity is greater than one. Moreover, the fraction of a floating object that is submerged equals its specific gravity. If an object’s specific gravity is exactly 1, then it will remain suspended in the fluid, neither sinking nor floating. Scuba divers try to obtain this state so that they can hover in the water. We measure the specific gravity of fluids, such as battery acid, radiator fluid, and urine, as an indicator of their condition. passages.before_xml: <para id="fs-id2397853">The coefficient of friction found in part (b) is much smaller than is typically found between tires and roads. Mass cancels because friction is assumed proportional to the normal force, which in turn is proportional to mass. items.title: Pressure work and sign conventions
items.reason: The existing note conflates internal/external pressure with opposite work-sign conventions. Replace the note with a consistent work-sign convention using the gas pressure acting on the piston, and scope the adjacent isothermal claim to an ideal gas. Piston acceleration does not invalidate the boundary-work calculation. Retain the parenthetical format and chemistry reference; no textbook structure changes are applied.

passages.before_xml: <para id="eip-763">An <term id="isothermal">isothermal process</term> is a thermodynamic process in which no change in temperature takes place. A gas expanding isothermally, for example, does work on the surrounding, but its internal energy (as represented by the temperature) does not change, because enough heat flows in to balance out the energy expended in doing work. This is consistent with the first law of thermodynamics (<m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:cn>0</m:cn><m:mrow><m:ci>Δ</m:ci><m:ci>U</m:ci></m:mrow><m:apply><m:minus/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:apply></m:math>, because <m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:ci>Q</m:ci><m:ci>W</m:ci></m:apply></m:math>). passages.proposed_xml: <para id="eip-763">An <term id="isothermal">isothermal process</term> is a thermodynamic process in which no change in temperature takes place. An isothermal process occurs if a thermodynamic process in a gas occurs slowly enough so that the gas remains in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding at all times.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737790371">How can we calculate the change in entropy for an irreversible process when <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>tot</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">+</m:mo><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:msub><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔS rSub { size 8{"tot"} } =ΔS rSub { size 8{h} } +ΔS rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is valid only for reversible processes? items.reason: First state only what the reservoir calculation establishes for one full cycle of a reversible Carnot engine, then complete the opening promise by accounting for the engine returning to its initial state. passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737860425">If we are interested in how heat transfer is converted into doing work, then the conservation of energy principle is important. The first law of thermodynamics applies the conservation of energy principle to systems where heat transfer and doing work are the methods of transferring energy into and out of the system. The <term id="import-auto-id1169737753839">first law of thermodynamics</term> states that the change in internal energy of a system equals the net heat transfer <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">into</emphasis></emphasis> the system minus the net work done <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">by</emphasis></emphasis> the system. In equation form, the first law of thermodynamics is</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737860425">If we are interested in how heat transfer is converted into doing work, then the conservation of energy principle is important. The first law of thermodynamics applies the conservation of energy principle to systems where heat transfer and doing work are the methods of transferring energy into and out of the system. A <emphasis effect="bold">closed system</emphasis> can exchange energy, but not matter, with its surroundings. An <emphasis effect="bold">isolated system</emphasis> exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings. Here we consider closed systems, with energy transferred by heat and work. The <term id="import-auto-id1169737753839">first law of thermodynamics</term> states that the change in internal energy of a system equals the net heat transfer <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">into</emphasis></emphasis> the system minus the net work done <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">by</emphasis></emphasis> the system. In equation form, the first law of thermodynamics is</para>
context_after_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737803043">Here <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔU} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the <emphasis effect="italics">change in internal energy</emphasis> <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> of the system. <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>Q</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">net heat transferred into the system</emphasis></emphasis>—that is, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>Q</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the sum of all heat transfer into and out of the system. <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">net work done by the system</emphasis></emphasis>—that is, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the sum of all work done on or by the system.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738182621">This result, which has general validity, means that <emphasis effect="italics">the total change in entropy for a system in any reversible process is zero.</emphasis></para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738182621">This result means <emphasis effect="italics">the total change in entropy of the surrounding</emphasis> for one full cycle of a reversible Carnot engine is zero. The engine itself returns to its initial state after one full cycle, so its entropy is unchanged. Thus, the total entropy change of the engine and its surroundings is zero.</para>
passages.authorization: Maintainer supplied the reservoir-only conclusion and approved the following explanation that the engine returns to its initial state; do not generalize this calculation to all reversible processes.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169736590877">The entropy of various parts of the system may change, but the total change is zero. Furthermore, the system does not affect the entropy of its surroundings, since heat transfer between them does not occur. Thus the reversible process changes neither the total entropy of the system nor the entropy of its surroundings. Sometimes this is stated as follows: <emphasis effect="italics">Reversible processes do not affect the total entropy of the universe.</emphasis> Real processes are not reversible, though, and they do change total entropy. We can, however, use hypothetical reversible processes to determine the value of entropy in real, irreversible processes. The following example illustrates this point.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169736590877">The entropy of the system and that of its surroundings may each change, but their changes sum to zero for a reversible process. Sometimes this is stated as follows: <emphasis effect="italics">Reversible processes do not affect the total entropy of the universe.</emphasis> Real processes are not reversible, though, and they do change total entropy. We can, however, use hypothetical reversible processes to determine the value of entropy in real, irreversible processes. The following example illustrates this point.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737821042"><emphasis effect="italics">There is an increase in entropy for any system undergoing an irreversible process.</emphasis></para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737821042"><emphasis effect="italics">There is an increase in entropy for the system and its surroundings together during an irreversible process.</emphasis></para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737871583">With respect to entropy, there are only two possibilities: entropy is constant for a reversible process, and it increases for an irreversible process. There is a fourth version of <term id="import-auto-id1169737036046">the second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy</term>:</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737871583">With respect to entropy, there are only two possibilities: the combined entropy of the system and its surroundings is constant for a reversible process and increases for an irreversible process. There is a fourth version of <term id="import-auto-id1169737036046">the second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy</term>:</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737795608">We can think about the internal energy of a system in two different but consistent ways. The first is the atomic and molecular view, which examines the system on the atomic and molecular scale. The <term id="import-auto-id1169737763498">internal energy</term> <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules. Recall that kinetic plus potential energy is called mechanical energy. Thus internal energy is the sum of atomic and molecular mechanical energy. Because it is impossible to keep track of all individual atoms and molecules, we must deal with averages and distributions. A second way to view the internal energy of a system is in terms of its macroscopic characteristics, which are very similar to atomic and molecular average values.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737795608">We can think about the internal energy of a system in two different but consistent ways. The first is the atomic and molecular view, which examines the system on the atomic and molecular scale. The <term id="import-auto-id1169737763498">internal energy</term> <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules. Recall that kinetic plus potential energy is called mechanical energy. Thus internal energy is the sum of atomic and molecular mechanical energy. Because it is impossible to keep track of all individual atoms and molecules, we must deal with averages and distributions.</para>
passages.authorization: Maintainer requested the suggested internal-energy/state-property replacement in context for preview review.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737754060">Macroscopically, we define the change in internal energy <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔU} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> to be that given by the first law of thermodynamics:</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737754060">A second way to view the internal energy of a system is in terms of its macroscopic characteristics, which are very similar to atomic and molecular average values. Internal energy is a property of the state of a system. For a fixed amount of an ideal gas, it depends only on temperature: raising the temperature increases the internal energy. For other materials, volume and physical state can also matter. For example, melting ice into water increases its internal energy even though its temperature remains constant during melting.</para>
passages.authorization: Maintainer requested the suggested internal-energy/state-property replacement in context for preview review.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738144580">Many detailed experiments have verified that <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>U</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">−</m:mo><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔU=Q - W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, where <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ΔU} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is the change in total kinetic and potential energy of all atoms and molecules in a system. It has also been determined experimentally that the internal energy <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> of a system depends only on the state of the system and <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">not how it reached that state</emphasis>.</emphasis> More specifically, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> is found to be a function of a few macroscopic quantities (pressure, volume, and temperature, for example), independent of past history such as whether there has been heat transfer or work done. This independence means that if we know the state of a system, we can calculate changes in its internal energy <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>U</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{U} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> from a few macroscopic variables.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738144580">The change in internal energy depends only on the initial and final states, whereas the amounts of heat transferred and work done depend on the process connecting those states.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738036913">Recall that the simple definition of energy is the ability to do work. Entropy is a measure of how much energy is not available to do work. That unavailable energy is of interest in thermodynamics, because the field of thermodynamics arose from efforts to convert heat to work.</para>

Remaining comparisons are proposals, not applied changes.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738013059">Heat pumps, air conditioners, and refrigerators utilize heat transfer from cold to hot. They are heat engines run backward. We say backward, rather than reverse, because except for Carnot engines, all heat engines, though they can be run backward, cannot truly be reversed. Heat transfer occurs from a cold reservoir <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> and into a hot one. This requires work input <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, which is also converted to heat transfer. Thus the heat transfer to the hot reservoir is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub><m:mo stretchy="false">+</m:mo><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{h} } =Q rSub { size 8{c} } +W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>. (Note that <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{h} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{W} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> are positive, with their directions indicated on schematics rather than by sign.) A heat pump’s mission is for heat transfer <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{h} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> to occur into a warm environment, such as a home in the winter. The mission of air conditioners and refrigerators is for heat transfer <emphasis effect="italics"/><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>c</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{Q rSub { size 8{c} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> to occur from a cool environment, such as chilling a room or keeping food at lower temperatures than the environment. (Actually, a heat pump can be used both to heat and cool a space. It is essentially an air conditioner and a heating unit all in one. In this section we will concentrate on its heating mode.)</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737723054">Since the efficiency of a heat engine is <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mstyle><m:mrow><m:mtext fontstyle="italic">Eff</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mstyle><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">/</m:mo><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mrow><m:mtext>h</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ ital "Eff"=W/Q rSub { size 8{h} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, we see that <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mstyle><m:mrow><m:msub><m:mtext fontstyle="italic">COP</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mtext>hp</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msub></m:mrow></m:mstyle><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mo stretchy="false">/</m:mo><m:mstyle><m:mrow><m:mtext fontstyle="italic">Eff</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mstyle></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ ital "COP" rSub { size 8{"hp"} } =1/ ital "Eff"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>, an important and interesting fact. passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737761565">Friction and other irreversible processes reduce heat engine efficiency, but they do <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">not</emphasis></emphasis> benefit the operation of a heat pump—instead, they reduce the work input by converting part of it to heat transfer back into the cold reservoir before it gets into the heat pump.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737761565">Friction and other irreversible processes reduce heat engine efficiency, but they do <emphasis effect="italics">not</emphasis> benefit the operation of a heat pump. This is part of what it means for a process to be irreversible. We can model these losses by letting only a portion <m:math><m:msup><m:mi>W</m:mi><m:mo>′</m:mo></m:msup></m:math> of the work input <m:math><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:math> reach a reversible heat pump, with the rest dissipated outside the hot reservoir. For the same heat delivery <m:math><m:msub><m:mi>Q</m:mi><m:mi>h</m:mi></m:msub></m:math> to the hot reservoir at the same reservoir temperatures, greater work input <m:math><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:math> is needed.</para>
passages.review_label: C. Model the loss of effective work input
passages.review_reason: Maintainer-drafted replacement retains the first sentence and models the losses as W reduced to W′ before entering a reversible pump. The model explicitly deposits the remaining energy outside the hot reservoir so it is not also counted in Q_h. Compare equal heat delivery at the same reservoir temperatures; this is an illustrative loss model, not a claim that every real heat pump dissipates losses at that location.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737818788">Entropy is very different from energy. Entropy is <emphasis effect="italics">not</emphasis> conserved but increases in all real processes. Reversible processes (such as in Carnot engines) are the processes in which the most heat transfer to work takes place and are also the ones that keep entropy constant. Thus we are led to make a connection between entropy and the availability of energy to do work.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737818788">Entropy is very different from energy. The total entropy of a system and its surroundings increases in irreversible processes. For engines operating between the same two heat reservoirs, reversible processes yield the most work for a given heat input and keep the combined entropy of the system and its surroundings constant. Thus we are led to make a connection between entropy and the availability of energy to do work.</para>

<note id="fs-id1169738116696"><label/>
      <title>Problem-Solving Strategies for Thermodynamics</title>
    <list id="fs-id1169737792783" list-type="enumerated" number-style="arabic"><item id="import-auto-id1169737786600"><emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">Examine the situation to determine whether heat, work, or internal energy are involved</emphasis>.</emphasis> Look for any system where the primary methods of transferring energy are heat and work. Heat engines, heat pumps, refrigerators, and air conditioners are examples of such systems.</item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169737929881"><emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">Identify the system of interest and draw a labeled diagram of the system showing energy flow.</emphasis></emphasis></item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169736654386"><emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">Identify exactly what needs to be determined in the problem (identify the unknowns)</emphasis>.</emphasis> A written list is useful. Maximum efficiency means a Carnot engine is involved. Efficiency is not the same as the coefficient of performance.</item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169737778543"><emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">Make a list of what is given or can be inferred from the problem as stated (identify the knowns)</emphasis>.</emphasis> Be sure to distinguish heat transfer into a system from heat transfer out of the system, as well as work input from work output. In many situations, it is useful to determine the type of process, such as isothermal or adiabatic.</item>

passages.before_xml: <para id="eip-745">Now consider what observer A sees happening. Since both lamps are the same distance from her in her reference frame and the train is moving to the right, she perceives the flash from the right-hand bulb occurring before the left-hand bulb.  Since in her frame, the flashes are not emitted at the same time, they also do not arrive at the same time. Here, a relative velocity between observers affects whether two events are observed to be simultaneous. <emphasis effect="italics">Simultaneity is not absolute.</emphasis> Note, however, that both A and B agree on the order of the flashes arriving at A’s location.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="eip-745">Now consider what observer A sees happening. As observer B also notes, she receives the flash from the right-hand bulb before the flash from the left-hand bulb. Since the lamps are equally distant from her and light travels at the same speed in both directions in her frame (postulate 2), she concludes that the right-hand bulb emitted its flash first. Here, a relative velocity between observers affects whether two events are observed to be simultaneous. <emphasis effect="italics">Simultaneity is not absolute.</emphasis></para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2998902">This illustrates the power of clear thinking. We might have guessed incorrectly that if light is emitted simultaneously, then two observers halfway between the sources would see the flashes simultaneously. But careful analysis shows this not to be the case. Einstein was brilliant at this type of <emphasis effect="italics"><emphasis effect="italics">thought experiment</emphasis></emphasis> (in German, “Gedankenexperiment”). He very carefully considered how an observation is made and disregarded what might seem obvious. The validity of thought experiments, of course, is determined by actual observation. The genius of Einstein is evidenced by the fact that experiments have repeatedly confirmed his theory of relativity.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2998902">This <emphasis effect="italics">thought experiment</emphasis> shows how the postulates of special relativity lead to a counterintuitive conclusion. We might expect two flashes emitted simultaneously for one observer to be emitted simultaneously for everyone. But the second postulate requires both observers to measure the same speed of light, despite their relative motion. Even after accounting for light-travel times, they disagree about whether the flashes were emitted simultaneously. Neither inertial reference frame is privileged (postulate 1), so we must give up the idea of absolute simultaneity.</para>
passages.authorization: Maintainer requested a substantial rewrite emphasizing the counterintuitive conclusions required by the SR postulates, especially the second postulate.

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1343207">As with all paradoxes, the premise is faulty and leads to contradictory conclusions. In fact, the astronaut’s motion is significantly different from that of the Earth-bound twin. The astronaut accelerates to a high velocity and then decelerates to view the star system. To return to the Earth, she again accelerates and decelerates. The Earth-bound twin does not experience these accelerations. So the situation is not symmetric, and it is not correct to claim that the astronaut will observe the same effects as her Earth-bound twin. If you use special relativity to examine the twin paradox, you must keep in mind that the theory is expressly based on inertial frames, which by definition are not accelerated or rotating. Einstein developed general relativity to deal with accelerated frames and with gravity, a prime source of acceleration. You can also use general relativity to address the twin paradox and, according to general relativity, the astronaut will age less. The key is that the twins follow different paths through spacetime, so they need not experience the same elapsed time.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1343207">During each constant-velocity leg of the journey, each twin measures the other’s clock as running slower. This symmetry does not extend to the whole round trip. The astronaut turns around and changes inertial frames, while the Earth-bound twin remains in approximately the same inertial frame. Changing frames also changes which event on Earth the astronaut assigns as simultaneous with her own: the outward and return frames assign different ages to the distant Earth-bound twin at the turnaround. Accounting for this change, special relativity predicts that the astronaut ages less when the twins reunite. The key is that the twins follow different paths through spacetime, so they need not experience the same elapsed time.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2722570">In 1971, American physicists Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating verified time dilation at low relative velocities by flying extremely accurate atomic clocks around the Earth on commercial aircraft. They measured elapsed time to an accuracy of a few nanoseconds and compared it with the time measured by clocks left behind. Hafele and Keating’s results were within experimental uncertainties of the predictions of relativity. Both special and general relativity had to be taken into account, since gravity and accelerations were involved as well as relative motion.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id2722570">In 1971, American physicists Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating verified time dilation at low relative velocities by flying extremely accurate atomic clocks around the Earth on commercial aircraft. They measured elapsed time to an accuracy of a few nanoseconds and compared it with the time measured by clocks left behind. Hafele and Keating’s results were within experimental uncertainties of the predictions of relativity. The predictions included both the effects of motion from special relativity and gravitational time dilation from general relativity: clocks at the aircraft’s higher altitude run faster than clocks on the ground because of the difference in gravitational potential.</para>

passages.proposed_xml: <item id="import-auto-id2574148">The twin paradox asks why a twin traveling at a relativistic speed away and then back towards the Earth ages less than the Earth-bound twin. Special relativity accounts for the different elapsed times along the twins’ paths.</item>

passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737795101">Compare the numbers of microstates for the two macrostates in <link target-id="import-auto-id1169738223876"/>. The macrostate with more microstates has greater entropy.</para>

passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737895337">The 60-heads, 40-tails macrostate has <m:math><m:mn>1.4</m:mn><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mn>10</m:mn><m:mn>28</m:mn></m:msup></m:math> microstates. The 50-heads, 50-tails macrostate has <m:math><m:mn>1.0</m:mn><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mn>10</m:mn><m:mn>29</m:mn></m:msup></m:math> microstates, about seven times as many. The entropy therefore increases.</para>

<para id="import-auto-id1169737967292">This increase in entropy means we have moved to a less orderly situation. It is not impossible for further tosses to produce the initial state of 60 heads and 40 tails, but it is less likely. There is about a 1 in 90 chance for that decrease in entropy (<m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">–</m:mo><m:mn>2</m:mn></m:mrow><m:mtext>.</m:mtext><m:mn>7</m:mn><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">–</m:mo><m:mtext>23</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext> J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{ +- 2 "." 7´"10" rSup { size 8{ +- "23"} } " J/K"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>) to occur. If we calculate the decrease in entropy to move to the most orderly state, we get <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mo stretchy="false">=</m:mo><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">–</m:mo><m:mtext>92</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">–</m:mo><m:mtext>23</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext> J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{DS= +- "92"´"10" rSup { size 8{ +- "23"} } " J/K"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>. There is about a <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mtext> in </m:mtext><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mtext>30</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{1" in ""10" rSup { size 8{"30"} } } {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> chance of this change occurring. So while very small decreases in entropy are unlikely, slightly greater decreases are impossibly unlikely. These probabilities imply, again, that for a macroscopic system, a decrease in entropy is impossible. For example, for heat transfer to occur spontaneously from 1.00 kg of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>0º</m:mn><m:mtext>C</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{0ºC} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> ice to its <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>0º</m:mn><m:mtext>C</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{0°C} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> environment, there would be a decrease in entropy of <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mtext>.</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mtext>22</m:mtext><m:mo stretchy="false">×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext> J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{1 "." "22" times "10" rSup { size 8{3} } " J/K"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>. Given that a <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>Δ</m:mn><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:msup><m:mtext> of 10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mo stretchy="false">–</m:mo><m:mtext>21</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext> J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{DS" of 10" rSup { size 8{ +- "21"} } " J/K"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math> corresponds to about a <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mn>1</m:mn><m:mtext> in </m:mtext><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mtext>30</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:msup></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> chance, a decrease of this size (<m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:mrow><m:msup><m:mtext>10</m:mtext><m:mrow><m:mn>3</m:mn></m:mrow></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext> J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:mrow><m:mrow/></m:mrow><m:annotation encoding="StarMath 5.0"> size 12{"10" rSup { size 8{3} } " J/K"} {}</m:annotation></m:semantics></m:math>) is an <emphasis effect="italics">utter</emphasis> impossibility. Even for a milligram of melted ice to spontaneously refreeze is impossible.</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169737967292">It is not impossible for further tosses to produce the initial state of 60 heads and 40 tails, but it is less likely than 50 heads and 50 tails. The coin model illustrates why a macrostate with more microstates is more likely. For a macroscopic physical system, a substantial spontaneous decrease in total entropy is overwhelmingly unlikely.</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738164157">(a) What is the change in entropy if you start with 100 coins in the 45 heads and 55 tails macrostate, toss them, and get 51 heads and 49 tails? (b) What if you get 75 heads and 25 tails? (c) How much more likely is 51 heads and 49 tails than 75 heads and 25 tails? (d) Does either outcome violate the second law of thermodynamics?</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738164157">(a) Does entropy increase or decrease if you start with 100 coins in the 45 heads and 55 tails macrostate, toss them, and get 51 heads and 49 tails? (b) Does entropy increase or decrease if you get 75 heads and 25 tails? (c) How much more likely is 51 heads and 49 tails than 75 heads and 25 tails? (d) Does either outcome violate the second law of thermodynamics?</para>

passages.before_xml: <para id="import-auto-id1169738072210">(a) What is the change in entropy if you start with 10 coins in the 5 heads and 5 tails macrostate, toss them, and get 2 heads and 8 tails? (b) How much more likely is 5 heads and 5 tails than 2 heads and 8 tails? (Take the ratio of the number of microstates to find out.) (c) If you were betting on 2 heads and 8 tails would you accept odds of 252 to 45? Explain why or why not.</para>

passages.before_xml:
<note id="fs-id1169738068841"><label/><title>Problem-Solving Strategies for Entropy</title>

    <list id="fs-id1169738116732" list-type="enumerated" number-style="arabic"><item id="import-auto-id1169738012863"><emphasis effect="italics">Examine the situation to determine if entropy is involved.</emphasis></item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169738249054"><emphasis effect="italics">Identify the system of interest and draw a labeled diagram of the system showing energy flow.</emphasis></item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169738249056"><emphasis effect="italics">Identify exactly what needs to be determined in the problem (identify the unknowns).</emphasis> A written list is useful.</item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169737769982"><emphasis effect="italics">Make a list of what is given or can be inferred from the problem as stated (identify the knowns).</emphasis> You must carefully identify the heat transfer, if any, and the temperature at which the process takes place. It is also important to identify the initial and final states.</item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169736622277"><emphasis effect="italics">Solve the appropriate equation for the quantity to be determined (the unknown).</emphasis> Note that the change in entropy can be determined between any states by calculating it for a reversible process.</item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169737951074"><emphasis effect="italics">Substitute the known value along with their units into the appropriate equation, and obtain numerical solutions complete with units.</emphasis></item>
    <item id="import-auto-id1169738138484"><emphasis effect="italics">To see if it is reasonable: Does it make sense?</emphasis> For example, total entropy should increase for any real process or be constant for a reversible process. Disordered states should be more probable and have greater entropy than ordered states.</item>
    </list></note>

items.title: Boltzmann constant notation: k_B
items.attention: Coordinated notation preview; maintainer requested book-wide reconciliation
items.reason: Use k_B consistently for Boltzmann’s constant, preserving numerical values and all other meanings of k. Includes definitions, worked equations, summaries, glossary, and appendix tables.

<list id="fs-id1169737713969"><item id="import-auto-id1169737780420">Disorder is far more likely than order, which can be seen statistically.</item>

<item>The entropy of a system in a given state (a macrostate) can be written as <equation id="eip-id1923841"><m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mi>S</m:mi><m:mo>=</m:mo><m:mi>k</m:mi><m:mn>ln</m:mn><m:mi>W</m:mi><m:mo>,</m:mo></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math></equation>
where

<m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mi>k</m:mi><m:mo>=</m:mo><m:mn>1.38</m:mn><m:mo>×</m:mo><m:msup><m:mn>10</m:mn><m:mn>–23</m:mn></m:msup><m:mspace width="0.25em"/><m:mtext>J/K</m:mtext></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math>  is Boltzmann’s constant, and <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mn>ln</m:mn><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math> is the natural logarithm of the number of microstates <m:math><m:semantics><m:mrow><m:mi>W</m:mi></m:mrow></m:semantics></m:math>  corresponding to the given macrostate.</item>
    </list>

passages.before_xml: <para id="eip-419"><link target-id="import-auto-id1169736581959"/> illustrates these three processes on a plot of pressure and volume (a <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> diagram). In an isothermal process, as the gas expands, the pressure decreases. This can be predicted from the ideal gas law (<m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:mrow><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:mrow><m:mrow><m:ci>N</m:ci><m:ci>k</m:ci><m:ci>T</m:ci></m:mrow></m:apply></m:math>). Since the temperature is constant, if volume increases, the pressure must decrease, to keep <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> constant. You can also see that in an adiabatic process, the pressure decreases with expanding volume more steeply than an isothermal process, because in an adiabatic process, the temperature is not constant, but it decreases. So with increasing <m:math><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math>, the pressure decrease even more rapidly, so that <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> actually decreases (for decreasing temperature).</para>
passages.proposed_xml: <para id="eip-419"><link target-id="import-auto-id1169736581959"/> illustrates these three processes on a plot of pressure and volume (a <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> diagram). In an isothermal process, as the gas expands, the pressure decreases. This can be predicted from the ideal gas law (<m:math><m:apply><m:eq/><m:mrow><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:mrow><m:mrow><m:ci>N</m:ci><m:msub><m:mi>k</m:mi><m:mi mathvariant="normal">B</m:mi></m:msub><m:ci>T</m:ci></m:mrow></m:apply></m:math>). Since the temperature is constant, if volume increases, the pressure must decrease, to keep <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> constant. You can also see that in an adiabatic process, the pressure decreases with expanding volume more steeply than an isothermal process, because in an adiabatic process, the temperature is not constant, but it decreases. So with increasing <m:math><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math>, the pressure decrease even more rapidly, so that <m:math><m:ci>P</m:ci><m:ci>V</m:ci></m:math> actually decreases (for decreasing temperature).</para>
